https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c980.text: Image source, Reuters By James Landale Diplomatic correspondent Published 5 hours ago The talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion. The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago. The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday. You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making. Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell. And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe. Image source, Reuters But fundamental differences remain. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield. The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded. Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army. After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult". Figure caption, Watch: President Zelensky welcomes US envoys in Kyiv Witkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there. But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that. So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead. Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Others are less optimistic. Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long. Photograph: Larry Downing/Reuters View image in fullscreen The CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs. Photograph: Larry Downing/Reuters September 11 2001 CIA releases dozens of presidential daily briefs on Bin Laden and al-Qaida from before 9/11 The presidential briefing documents were declassified on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks Associated Press Fri 11 Sep 2026 18.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Several dozen presidential briefing documents declassified on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks , detail intelligence that government officials had gathered about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaida leading up to the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and upended American national security . The documents illustrate security analysts’ tracking of Bin Laden’s movements and support system, as well as concerns about possible threats to US targets. They also detail officials’ understanding of his network in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were financed. Proclaiming it “an act of exceptional transparency”, the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs – the highly classified briefings prepared by the nation’s intelligence community for the government’s most senior leaders. Trump and Hegseth use 9/11 memorial remarks at Pentagon to defend war on Iran Read more The documents range from a February 1998 file – prepared for then president Bill Clinton – titled “Terrorists seeking WMD capability” and mentioning Bin Laden and other Islamic extremists – to a 12 September 2001 report in which a source indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the US Capitol. An April 1998 document described the Taliban’s unwillingness to hand over Bin Laden, at the time seen as their “guest” in Afghanistan , noting their “gratitude for his assistance during the Soviet occupation” was making them “reluctant to alienate him by monitoring or controlling his activities”. Briefers in July 1998 called it “plausible that Bin Ladin places a high priority on conducting attacks in the United States” and noted his “interest in conducting attacks with chemical and biological agents”. Two months later, a briefer wrote that Bin Laden’s “preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington”, and that al-Qaida “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”. Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described how conspirators “had evaded security checks during a recent trial run at an unidentified New York airport”, and “some members of the Bin Ladin network have received hijack training”. Other documents detail Bin Laden’s pursuit of materials for making “dirty bombs”, conventional weapons infused with radioactive material. By June 1999, according to intelligence officials, his operatives had conducted such experiments with explosives to “increase their energy output”. About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials were aware that Bin Laden appeared to be misleading the Taliban about his reluctance to launch an unprovoked attack on the US. Briefs prepared for George W Bush in early 2001 focused in part on Bin Laden’s “experimentation by crude means to make and deploy biological agents”. A report a month before the attacks indicated Bin Laden’s commitment “to conduct terrorist attacks in the US”, noting that the 1998 al-Qaida attacks on US embassies “demonstrate that he prepares operations years in advance and is not deterred by setbacks”. At that time – August 2001 – officials wrote of “suspicious activity in this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York”, adding that the FBI was “conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the US that it considers Bin Ladin-related”. Many of the documents were redacted to conceal sources’ names and other identifying information. They didn’t appear to break any new ground on the planning of the attacks or on US officials’ understanding of how they had unfolded. In the years immediately after the attacks, a bipartisan commission highlighted a lack of information-sharing among agencies such as the CIA and FBI, and issued recommendations that yielded new positions, including a centralized director of national intelligence, as well as the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes domestic and foreign terrorism information across different government branches. Asked for comment on the release, the White House noted the release of another batch of documents by the National Archives, also on Friday. That batch, including interviews with national security officials in the Clinton and Bush administrations, was a product of the commission that investigated the attacks from 2002 to 2004. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: The consulate general’s diplomats are part of an independent team who report directly to London. Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA View image in fullscreen The consulate general’s diplomats are part of an independent team who report directly to London. Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA Israel Analysis Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem Consulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the city Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.16 EDT Last modified on Thu 8 Oct 2026 13.40 EDT Share Israel’s attempt to close the British consulate general in Jerusalem was primarily designed to deter London from imposing sanctions on settlements in occupied Palestine . But it also served the current government’s ambitions to fully annex Jerusalem as a national capital, diplomatic and legal experts said. The UK mission to the city has an unusual diplomatic status, which dates back to before the founding of the state of Israel , rooted in a vision of Jerusalem as a neutral enclave under international control. Unlike other consulates general around the world, it is not a satellite of the British embassy in Tel Aviv. Instead its diplomats are part of an independent team, who report directly to London. British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband Read more That is anathema to those in Israel who claim all of Jerusalem as their territory. Israeli forces occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, and the Knesset passed a law annexing the city in 1980, but that status has not been recognised by most of the world. Gideon Sa’ar, the Israeli foreign minister, threatened to close the consulate general a month ago in an attempt to deter the UK government from proceeding with plans to bar trade with West Bank settlements and put sanctions on companies that provide them with services including financing. The UK threatened to respond with a mass expulsion of diplomats but the two countries appear to have backed away from a full-blown diplomatic spat as Israel prepares for national elections, due on 27 October. Britain will rebrand its consulate general ⁠as a UK “mission” and reduce the number of diplomats, but it will remain independent of Tel Aviv in a compromise one source described as a temporary “ceasefire”. If Israel gets a new leader in three weeks, negotiations on the status of the consulate and its staff could resume. Maintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, said Daniel Seidemann, an Israeli lawyer and expert in the geopolitics of Jerusalem who has advised western diplomats including a British foreign secretary. “The arrangement that the UK arrived at with Israel was probably the optimal among a number of options that were even worse. So I’m not faulting anybody, but this is far from a victory,” he said. “ The British presence in Jerusalem after almost a century and a half has been downgraded from one of the diplomatic mission to another office. And that is a stark qualitative change.” View image in fullscreen Maintaining a foothold in Jerusalem and the independent status of UK diplomats was important, one expert said. Photograph: Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu/Getty Images There are seven other consulates general in East Jerusalem, all opened before 1948, representing their nations’ interests in Jerusalem and occupied Palestine. Like the UK one, they are independent and report directly to their foreign ministries. They have long been a particular thorn in Israel’s side because of their unusual status, which reflects the designation of Jerusalem as “corpus separatum”, an independent body, under the UN’s 1947 partition plan for historic Palestine. Never implemented, it envisaged Jerusalem as a sort of Vatican-like independent enclave, under international administration. That clashes with Israel’s claim on the city, and Sa’ar’s attack on the consulate should be seen in that context, and not purely as a response to sanctions. “ This is part of the overall attempt to establish the primacy of a very specific Jewish-Israeli Jerusalem,” Seidemann said. “Any diplomatic presence in Jerusalem that does not pay fealty to the government of Israel and Israel’s sole sovereignty is targeted.” Other countries have missions based in Ramallah to manage relations with Palestinians, but these are technically subsidiary to Tel Aviv embassies. The US had a consulate general but closed it after Donald Trump recognised Jerusalem as the capital of Israel during his first presidency. The UK sanctions plan represents the most consequential attempt by one of Israel’s allies to halt settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. Israeli banks are rattled by a proposal they fear could affect their business, Haaretz reported on Thursday. An assessment by Israel’s Association of Banks laid out concerns that they could be affected, and they are refusing to say whether they will provide financial guarantees needed to underpin construction contracts for the E1 settlement in the West Bank . When Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, announced his plans, he said the timing was driven partly by the Israeli government’s decision to put out tenders for this project. Israel’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has boasted that it will “bury” the possibility of a Palestinian state by severing parts of the occupied West Bank. Ilan Baruch, a former Israeli ambassador to South Africa, left diplomatic service to advocate for a two-state solution, including pushing foreign governments to move beyond condemnations of Israeli policy to imposing a “meaningful price”. The threats to Britain’s Jerusalem consulate were a sign the UK had finally done that. “I was relieved [by Israel’s position], realising Miliband touched a nerve,” he said. Renaming the consulate while preserving its independent status indicated Israel had stepped back from confrontation, helped by Britain making smaller “face-saving” concessions, he said. https://www.liverpoolecho.co.uk/whats-on.text: A last minute anniversary trip to the Baltic region of northern Europe proved far more appealing than it's infamous industrial nature would suggest. Latvia was never particularly high on my list of dreamy getaways, but Riga offered everything and more. From its striking Art Nouveau architecture and historic Old Town filled with charming cafés to its effortlessly beautiful streets, it was a city with everything we didn't know we needed. I only spent a weekend in Riga , but it’s a city already drawing me back for a longer stay. I've never known any friends to visit, so consider this an insider recommendation for a destination that most people - myself included - would never have thought to rank so highly among their travel recommendations. As of writing, there are no direct flights to Riga - or any Latvia destination - from Liverpool John Lennon Airport . You will have to travel to Manchester for your departure. The flight time between Manchester and Riga is approximately two hours and 30 minutes, with a two hour time zone change. The only airline delivering flights is Ryanair. The best attractions in Riga are free! The Old Town is the most obvious, demanding the vast majority of your time with its cobbled streets and historic buildings easy to lose yourself among. Dead centre is Riga Cathedral, towering over its neighbours, with other notable structures including St Peter's church and the quirky Three Brothers houses. If you're searching for the Riga tourist sign, it's popped in front of the House of Blackheads landmark. Luckily, the bottom of the building boasts an affordable souvenir shop for all your holiday trinkets. The Latvian War Museum, the Occupation Museum and the Museum of Art are all free, so take your time to explore. There's also river boat trips through the Old Town and to the edge of the city for a measly €12. The Freedom Monument and Panorama Tower should be on the list for architecture buffs. The latter even has a viewing deck for the best view of the city. Latvia is rich in authentic Baltic food so if you're the inquisitive type with a hankering for freshly caught seafood, then you're in luck. Uncle Vanya is one of the best in town, but you'll find great spots everywhere. Riga is great for tourists. English is the country's second language and widely spoken in the city centre and key tourist areas. You won't have to worry about a language barrier as most of your interactions will begin in English, with English menus and signs readily available. Riga is fairly affordable, and hotel prices won't burn a hole in your bank account. You won't need to travel around by bus or tram either, as all of the hotspots are within walking distance from the city centre. Before arriving, I imagined Latvia would offer more or less the same as its northern neighbour, Estonia; a charming Old Town surrounded by less-than-charming buildings. And hey, I wouldn't have minded. But what I got was a city brimming with beautiful architecture for miles. The parks along the Daugava River looked like something straight off a postcard, with every stereotypical autumn scene you could dream of. When we weren't busy falling in love with the scenery, we were happily eating our way through the city, popping into all the cute cafés and little shops along the way. We visited quite a few actually, including the decadent Black Magic truffle and cake café with secret entrances with a mystical, apothecary aesthetic. The aforementioned Uncle Vanya's restaurant was our date night stop for a gluttonous array of Latvian home cooked classics, including sturgeon balyk, fish solyanka and pelmeni. The highest cocktail bar in the city Skyline, atop of the Radisson Hotel building, may seem glamorous, but I would give it a miss. It's not all it's marked up to be in terms of views, service or experience. The evening offered just as much fun as the daytime with plenty of bars to keep us entertained until late. If you like karaoke, you'll find a venue to sing your heart out on every street. At one point, we counted eight in an approximate two minute walk. If you see a bar, it's probably a karaoke bar. If I had known how much I would've enjoyed Riga I would've stayed for longer. For now, it's firmly on my list of destinations to revisit.
